summary: Defines the protocol and the MIB for collecting response-time data on TN3270 and TN3270E sessions by a TN3270E server.

eli5.summary: This is a stopwatch for mainframe terminal sessions, measuring how long the computer takes to answer a person at the keyboard.

questions: what is the tn3270e rt mib
how does tn3270e measure response time
what is a definite response in sna
subtitle: How a TN3270E server times mainframe terminal transactions and exposes the results through SNMP.

tldr.problem: Operators of 3270 terminal services need response time data to check service level agreements and watch performance, but not every TN3270E server has access to SNA response time monitoring.
tldr.mechanism: The server takes timestamps as a request, its reply and the client's definite response (or a TIMING-MARK reply) pass through it, then keeps sliding-window averages and five response time buckets in the TN3270E-RT-MIB.
tldr.outcome: Management applications can read total and IP-network response times per client group and receive notifications when averages cross thresholds.

today: RFC 2562 is a Proposed Standard from April 1999 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the TN3270E-MIB in RFC 2561.

sections.title: Purpose and Prerequisites
sections.content:
RFC 2562 defines a protocol and a MIB module that let a TN3270E server collect and keep response time data for both TN3270 and TN3270E clients. The data is structured to support validation of service level agreements and performance monitoring.

It builds on the TN3270E-MIB from RFC 2561, the TN3270E RFCs such as RFC 2355, and the Telnet Timing Mark option from RFC 860.
sections.eli5: It adds a stopwatch to the mainframe terminal middleman, plus a place to read the times.

sections.title: How Response Times Are Measured
sections.content:
SNA networks offer two ways to measure response time: the SNA/MS Response Time Monitoring (RTM) function, and timestamping using definite responses. This memo uses definite responses, because not all TN3270E server implementations have access to their underlying SNA stacks. It keeps the RTM ideas of response time buckets and interval-based collection.

The server saves timestamp D when a client request arrives, E when the target host replies, and F when the client answers the definite response (DR) that came with the reply. If the host did not ask for DR, the server may add its own and does not pass the answer on. From these:

  • Total response time is F minus D.
  • IP network transit time is F minus E.

Both are approximations, since the client's final response stands in for the request that started the transaction. This needs a TN3270E client with the RESPONSES function negotiated. A client SHOULD respond to a DR when it completes processing, otherwise its times look lower than they were. Printer sessions are excluded, and so are transactions where the host answers with UNBIND.
sections.eli5: The middleman notes the time when you press Enter, when the computer answers, and when your screen says it got the answer. The gaps between those notes are the response times.

sections.title: Timestamps, DR and TIMING-MARK
sections.content:
Timestamp D is taken when the server has received client data it can forward immediately. Host replies may come as several SNA request units in a chain. The server's only chance to ask the client for DR is on the first-in-chain unit, so some servers routinely specify DR on all of them. Timestamp E is taken when the last-in-chain unit is forwarded, and the server SHOULD take it as close as possible to its Telnet edge. Timestamp F is taken when the client's RESPONSES response arrives.

For TN3270 clients, or TN3270E clients without RESPONSES, the server can send a Telnet TIMING-MARK request after the last-in-chain unit instead. Then IP network time is F' minus E', and total time is (E minus D) plus (F' minus E'). The client cannot have the NOP option enabled. A server MUST NOT send a second TIMING-MARK while waiting for the first, and SHOULD spread requests out rather than send a burst.

The memo also shows how the server's IP-network component can be compared with timestamps taken by a monitor at the SNA host, so that SNA and IP transit times can be separated.
sections.eli5: If the screen cannot say it got the answer, the middleman can instead poke it with a quick ping and time how long the reply to the poke takes.

sections.title: Collection Control Options
sections.content:
Each tn3270eRtCollCtlEntry is indexed by a server and a client group, and its tn3270eRtCollCtlType object is a set of BITS: aggregate(0), excludeIpComponent(1), ddr(2), average(3), buckets(4) and traps(5). Either average or buckets MUST be set for data to be collected.

All transactions in an aggregate must contribute in the same way. If the IP component is included, transactions for which it cannot be calculated are left out altogether. If it is excluded, only the SNA-network component counts, and the server sets F equal to E. Dynamic definite responses (ddr) add DR requests so that more transactions can be included, but are ignored when the IP component is excluded.

Once an entry is active, only tn3270eRtCollCtlThreshHigh, tn3270eRtCollCtlThreshLow and the RowStatus may be set.
sections.eli5: A set of on and off switches decides what is timed, whether the network part counts, and whether to keep averages, a tally chart, or send alerts.

sections.title: Averages, Buckets and Notifications
sections.content:
Averages are sliding-window, which is often more meaningful and causes less notification thrashing. The sample period SPeriod defaults to 20 seconds and the multiplier SPMult to 30, giving a default collection interval of 10 minutes. The server updates sliding counters each period by adding the new value and subtracting the old value divided by SPMult.

A tn3270eRtExceeded notification is sent the first time a statistically significant average passes the high threshold, and not again until an average falls below the low threshold, when tn3270eRtOkay is sent. Significance depends on the average: the server notifies if AvgCountTrans * ((AvgRt/ThreshHigh - 1) ** 2) >= IdleCount. The RFC's example uses IdleCount 20 and a 200 msec threshold.

The buckets option uses four boundaries and five buckets. A bucket counts transactions at or below its boundary but above the previous one, and the fifth has no upper limit. The defaults are 1, 2, 5 and 10 seconds, taken from the 3174 controller's RTM implementation.
sections.eli5: Averages smooth out the ups and downs so one slow moment does not set off an alarm. Buckets are like tally columns for fast, medium and slow answers.

sections.title: Tables and Security
sections.content:
The MIB has tn3270eRtCollCtlTable for control and tn3270eRtDataTable for results. One data row exists for an aggregate collection, or one per client if not aggregated. The data table holds averages, counters, sums of squares for variance calculations, five bucket counters and a discontinuity time object that shows when counters may have been reset. tn3270eRtDataRtMethod says whether the IP time came from definite response or TIMING-MARK. Notifications cover collection start and end as well as the exceeded and okay events, and a spin lock object coordinates changes.

The security section matches RFC 2561: sensitive data calls for authenticated SNMP and access control, and without those the listed control objects should be read-only.
sections.eli5: One table holds the settings and another holds the results, like a settings screen and a scoreboard.

viz.caption: TIMESTAMPS D, E AND F AT THE SERVER

items.label: aggregate
items.desc: One data row for the whole client group instead of one per client.

items.label: excludeIpComponent
items.desc: Leave the IP-network part out of response times.

items.label: ddr
items.desc: Add definite response requests so more transactions can be timed.

items.label: buckets
items.desc: Count transactions into response time buckets.
